claim: The C. elegans nervous system contains twice as many GABA-positive neuron classes as previously reported.
source: We report here a comprehensive map of neurons in the C. elegans nervous system that contain the neurotransmitter GABA, revealing twice as many GABA-positive neuron classes as previously reported.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states that the study reveals twice as many GABA-positive neuron classes as previously reported, which is a primary finding of the manuscript.

claim: Previously, 26 C. elegans neurons falling into six neuron classes were identified as GABAergic.
source: Previous studies have ascribed a GABAergic neurotransmitter identity to 26 C. elegans neurons, which fall into six anatomically and functionally diverse neuron classes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous work (McIntire et al., 1993a, 1993b; Schuske et al., 2004) that identified these neurons.

claim: The previously identified GABAergic neuron classes are RME, AVL, RIS, DVB, DD, and VD.
source: The previously reported set of GABAergic neurons (six neuron classes: RME, AVL, RIS, DVB, DD, VD; Table 1) were defined by anti-GABA antibody staining and expression of reporter transgenes that monitor expression of genes that encode the GABA biosynthetic enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD/UNC-25) and the vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT/UNC-47) (Jin et al., 1999; McIntire et al., 1993b, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and is corroborated by the data in Table 1.

claim: Seven additional neuronal cell types were newly identified as GABA-positive: RIB, SMDD/V, AVB, AVA, AVJ, ALA, and AVF.
source: Using a modified GABA staining protocol, we observed the presence of GABA in the six previously described GABAergic neuron classes RME, AVL, RIS, VD, DD and DVB, but also detected staining in an additional set of seven neuronal cell types (RIB, SMDD/V, AVB, AVA, AVJ, ALA, AVF; Table 1, Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by anti-GABA staining data shown in Figure 1 and summarized in Table 1.

claim: GABA staining in newly identified GABA-positive cells is generally weaker than in previously identified GABA neurons.
source: Staining of these newly identified GABA-positive cells is generally weaker than in the previously identified GABA neurons (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This observation is based on comparison of staining intensity in Figure 1A,B.

claim: Anti-GABA staining in all cells is completely abolished in unc-25 mutant animals.
source: Anti-GABA staining in all cells, including the newly identified cells, is completely abolished in animals lacking the unc-25 gene which codes GABA-synthesizing enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase, thereby corroborating that the staining indeed reports on the presence of GABA (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 1C showing absence of GABA staining in unc-25 mutants.

claim: The AVJ neuron pair stains more strongly for GABA in larval stages compared to adult stages.
source: The same pattern of staining is observed in early larvae and adult worm, with the sole exception of the AVJ neuron pair which stains more strongly in larval compared to adult stages.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing GABA staining at different developmental stages.

claim: The ALA and AVF neurons are GABA uptake neurons that do not synthesize GABA but take it up from the extracellular environment.
source: We find that GABA staining of the ALA and AVF neurons is abolished in either unc-47 mutants (no GABA release from other neurons) or snf-11 mutants (no GABA uptake), further corroborating that these neurons do not synthesize their own GABA, but obtain synaptically released GABA by uptake via the plasma membrane transporter SNF-11/GAT (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA staining in unc-47 and snf-11 mutants (Figure 1D,E) and expression of snf-11 reporter in these neurons.

claim: The AVF neuron is a GABA clearance neuron that takes up GABA but does not re-release it.
source: We could not detect unc-47 fosmid reporter expression in the AVF neurons, which do not synthesize but only take up GABA, indicating that these neurons may only function to clear, but not re-release GABA.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of unc-47/VGAT expression in AVF neurons despite their GABA-positive staining and snf-11 expression.

claim: The ALA neuron is a GABA recycling neuron that takes up GABA and may re-release it.
source: We speculate that these neurons are possible 'GABA recycling neurons' that synaptically release GABA after uptake. The ALA neuron class falls into this category.
evidence: This is based on ALA expressing both snf-11/GAT (for uptake) and unc-47/VGAT (for vesicular release).

claim: The AVF neuron takes up GABA from D-type motor neurons.
source: To test this notion experimentally, we removed GABA selectively from D-type motor neurons, using the unc-30 mutant strain in which D-type motor neurons fail to produce GABA (Jin et al., 1994). In these animals GABA staining in AVF is abolished (Figure 1F), suggesting that AVF indeed absorbs GABA from the D-type motor neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally by loss of GABA staining in AVF in unc-30 mutants (Figure 1F).

claim: The ALA neuron may absorb GABA released by the SMD neurons.
source: However, as assessed by the examination of electron micrographs produced by White et al., the processes of ALA are directly adjacent to the newly identified GABAergic SMD neurons (White et al., 1986) (S. Cook, pers.comm.). This indicates that ALA may absorb GABA released by the SMD neurons, thereby modulating GABA transmission between SMD and its target neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from anatomical proximity of ALA and SMD processes based on electron microscopy data.

claim: Prevention of GABA release in unc-47/VGAT mutants results in increased GABA staining in SMDD and SMDV neurons.
source: Consistent with this notion, we find that prevention of GABA release in unc-47/VGAT mutants results in a considerable increase in GABA staining in the SMDD and SMDV neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by increased GABA staining in SMD neurons in unc-47 mutants shown in Figure 1D.

claim: GABA is detected in three classes of non-neuronal cells: the head mesodermal cell (hmc), the glia-like GLR cells, and body wall muscle.
source: In addition to neuronal staining, we also detected GABA in three classes of non-neuronal cells, the head mesodermal cell (hmc), the glia-like GLR cells and body wall muscle (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by anti-GABA staining shown in Figure 1A.

claim: GABA expression in non-neuronal cells depends on unc-25/GAD.
source: Expression in all these cells depends on unc-25/GAD (Figure 1C; note that residual staining remains in body wall muscle, perhaps an indication of alternative GABA-synthesis pathways; [Kim et al., 2015]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA staining in these cells in unc-25 mutants (Figure 1C).

claim: The hmc (head mesodermal cell) operates as a GABA clearance cell.
source: We indeed find that hmc expresses the GABA uptake transporter snf-11/GAT (Figure 2D) and that GABA staining of the hmc is abolished in snf-11/GAT mutants (Figure 1E). We also find that GABA staining in the hmc is reduced in unc-30 mutants (in which D-type motor neurons fail to be specified; [Jin et al., 1994]), indicating that the sources of GABA in the hmc are indeed the D-type motor neurons. Since we do not detect unc-47/VGAT expression in the hmc, the hmc likely operates as a GABA clearance cell, like the AVF neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from snf-11 expression, loss of GABA staining in snf-11 mutants, and absence of unc-47 expression in hmc.

claim: The GLR cells are glia-like cells that take up GABA.
source: The glia-like GLR cells are another intriguing GABA-positive cell type. GLR cells, which have no assigned function yet, are located directly adjacent to the nerve ring (http://www.wormatlas.org/ver1/handbook/mesodermal.htm/glr.htm). Each GLR cell extends a thin, sheet-like process that lies inside the nerve ring. Like the AVF and ALA neurons and the non-neuronal hmc, the GLR cells express snf-11/GAT (Figure 2) and GABA-staining is strongly reduced in snf-11/GAT mutants (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by snf-11 expression and loss of GABA staining in snf-11 mutants.

claim: GABA may pass from RME neurons to GLR cells through gap junctions in unc-47/VGAT mutants.
source: Curiously, staining is still observed in unc-47/VGAT mutants. In these mutants, GABA may accumulate in RME neurons which are heavily gap-junctioned with the GLR glia cells (White et al., 1986) and GABA may pass through these gap junctions.
evidence: This is inferred from persistence of GABA staining in GLR in unc-47 mutants and known gap junction connectivity between RME and GLR.

claim: Seven male-specific neurons are GABA-positive: EF1-4, R2A, R6A, and R9B.
source: In males, we observed the same set of GABA-positive neurons as observed in hermaphrodites. In addition, GABA staining is observed in one prominent class of male-specific interneurons , the EF neurons, which had previously no neurotransmitter assigned (Figure 3B). The EF1 and EF2 interneurons are located in the dorsorectal ganglion, whereas EF3 and the rarely generated EF4 are in the preanal ganglion (Figure 3B). The EF neurons are so-called 'type II interneurons', which relay sensory information from male-specific tail sensory structures into the sex-shared nervous system in the head (Jarrell et al., 2012). All the EF neurons also express unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT and snf-11/GAT, demonstrating that these neurons synthesize, release and reuptake GABA (Figure 3D). Apart from the EF neurons, three additional male-specific sensory neurons stain with anti-GABA antibodies, the R2A, R6A and R9B pairs of ray neurons (Figure 3B), but like the head AVA, AVB and AVJ, these neurons do not express unc-25/GAD and only R6A expresses unc-47/VGAT.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anti-GABA staining and reporter gene expression in male-specific neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: The EF neurons synthesize, release, and reuptake GABA.
source: All the EF neurons also express unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT and snf-11/GAT, demonstrating that these neurons synthesize, release and reuptake GABA (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by expression of unc-25, unc-47, and snf-11 reporters in EF neurons shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There is sexual dimorphism in snf-11/GAT expression in the VD12 neuron.
source: Lastly, we noted an intriguing sexual dimorphism of snf-11/GAT expression in the VD12 neuron, which is generated in both sexes and produces GABA in both sexes, based on unc-25/GAD expression and GABA staining. In hermaphrodites, none of the 13 VD neurons express snf-11/GAT, but in males, VD12 expresses snf-11/GAT (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by snf-11 reporter expression in VD12 in males but not hermaphrodites shown in Figure 3.

claim: 47 neuron classes are innervated by GABA(+); UNC-47(+) neurons.
source: Of the 118 anatomically defined neuron classes of the hermaphrodite, 47 neuron classes are innervated by GABA(+); UNC-47(+) neurons (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of synaptic connectivity data from the C. elegans wiring diagram.

claim: The RIB and SMD neurons are the GABAergic neurons with the most synaptic outputs.
source: The RIB and SMD neurons are the GABAergic neurons with the most synaptic outputs (Table 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of synaptic connectivity data shown in Table 3.

claim: The RIB and SMD neurons employ both GABA and ACh as neurotransmitters.
source: Both neurons also employ ACh as a neurotransmitter, even though in each case, one neurotransmitter system appears to predominate: The RIB neurons express barely detectable levels of VAChT/ChAT (Pereira et al., 2015), while their GABA staining is easily detectable. Conversely, the SMD neurons strongly express VAChT/ChAT (Pereira et al., 2015), but their GABA content is comparatively weak and variable.
evidence: This is based on expression data for GABA and ACh pathway genes in these neurons.

claim: The lgc-37 and gab-1 genes are located in a head-to-head orientation and share regulatory elements.
source: Of particular note is the head-to-head orientation of the alpha-subunit-encoding lgc-37 gene and the beta subunit-encoding gab-1 gene (Figure 4B); strikingly, this genomic organization is conserved from nematodes to vertebrates (Darlison et al., 2005; Tsang et al., 2007). This organization suggests that both genes employ the same cis-regulatory elements to ensure co-expression.
evidence: This is based on genomic organization shown in Figure 4B and cited literature on conservation.

claim: lgc-37 and gab-1 fosmid reporters are co-expressed in 25 neuron classes.
source: As expected by their above mentioned genomic organization, lgc-37 and gab-1 fosmid reporters are indeed co-expressed in 25 neuron classes (Table 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression data shown in Table 4.

claim: The AVE command interneuron is the only neuron that expresses the gab-1 fosmid reporter but not the lgc-37 fosmid reporter.
source: The only neuron where just one of the two fosmid reporters is expressed in, gab-1, is the AVE command interneuron (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by reporter gene expression shown in Figure 4F.

claim: GABAA-type receptors are expressed in neurons that are not anatomically connected to GABA-positive neurons.
source: In addition to being expressed in neurons that show anatomic innervation by GABAergic neurons, it is clearly evident that GABAA-type receptors are also expressed in neurons that are not anatomically connected to GABA-positive neurons (Figure 4B–D, white labels; all neurons listed in Table 4). These receptors may simply not function as GABA receptors or, more interestingly, these receptors may mediate GABA spillover transmission, a phenomenon observed in the vertebrate CNS as well as in C. elegans (Jobson et al., 2015; Rossi and Hamann, 1998).
evidence: This is based on GABA receptor expression patterns shown in Figure 4 and Table 4 compared to synaptic connectivity data.

claim: The Tailless/Tlx orphan nuclear receptor nhr-67 controls GABAergic identity of RME, AVL, and RIS neurons.
source: Sarin et al. have previously shown that the Tailless/Tlx orphan nuclear receptor nhr-67 is expressed in the GABAergic RMEs, RIS and AVL neurons and that nhr-67 expression is maintained in these neurons throughout adulthood in the RME and RIS neurons (Sarin et al., 2009). Consistent with a possible role of nhr-67 as a regulator of GABAergic identity, it was also reported that loss of nhr-67 affected expression of unc-47/VGAT in RME, AVL and RIS (Sarin et al., 2009). However, whether nhr-67 affects GABA synthesis, or the expression of other GABAergic identity features was not tested. We first isolated an unambiguous molecular null allele of nhr-67, ot795, using Mos transposon-mediated gene deletion (MosDEL; see Experimental Procedures) (Figure 5A). nhr-67(ot795) animals display an embryonic/L1 arrest phenotype. We stained these null mutant animals for GABA and examined unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT and unc-46/LAMP expression in these mutants. We found abnormalities in the expression of all markers in all three, normally nhr-67-expressing neuron classes, AVL, RME and RIS (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA pathway gene expression in nhr-67 mutants shown in Figure 5B.

claim: nhr-67 and lim-6 collaborate in the specification of AVL GABAergic identity.
source: Since nhr-67 null mutants did not display fully penetrant defects in the AVL and RIS neurons, we tested whether nhr-67 and lim-6 may collaborate in the specification of these neurons. We find that in nhr-67; lim-6 double null mutants, the AVL neurons show synergistic defects in the GABAergic identity specification (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by enhanced defects in nhr-67; lim-6 double mutants shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The LIM homeobox gene lim-6 controls GABA identity of RIS, AVL, and DVB neurons.
source: The LIM homeobox gene lim-6 was found to control unc-25 expression in the RIS, AVL and DVB neurons (Hobert et al., 1999). We corroborated the impact of lim-6 on GABA identity by anti-GABA staining of lim-6 null mutant animals (which had not previously been done), finding that GABA staining is affected in AVL, RIS and DVB (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA staining in lim-6 mutants shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The Prd-type homeobox gene ceh-10 controls GABAergic identity of RMED neurons.
source: ceh-10 was found to affect GABA staining and unc-25/GAD expression in the RMED neurons (where ceh-10 was reported to be expressed) (Forrester et al., 1998; Huang et al., 2004). We extended this previous finding by demonstrating that in ceh-10 mutants, not only the unc-25/GAD reporter, but also the unc-47/VGAT, unc-46/LAMP and snf-11/GAT reporters fail to be expressed in RMED (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA pathway gene expression in ceh-10 mutants shown in Figure 5E.

claim: ceh-10 does not affect the generation of RMED neurons.
source: Absence of expression of these reporters is not reflective of lineage defects, since we find that in ceh-10 hypomorphic mutants in which GABA staining is also severely affected, the RMED neurons are nevertheless formed, as assessed by the intact expression of a pan-neuronal marker (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by persistence of pan-neuronal marker expression in RMED in ceh-10 mutants shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The homeobox gene tab-1 controls GABAergic identity of RMEL/R neurons.
source: We identified a mutant allele, ot796, in which unc-47 failed to be expressed in the left and right RME neurons. Whole genome sequencing revealed that ot796 contains a splice site mutation in the tab-1 locus (Figure 6A; Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Table 5). The ot796 mutant allele fails to complement the GABA differentiation defects of other mutant alleles of tab-1 and three additional alleles of tab-1 display similar unc-47 expression defects as ot796 (Table 5). tab-1 mutants also fail to properly express unc-25 and unc-46 in RMEL/R and fail to antibody-stain for GABA (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA pathway gene expression in tab-1 mutants shown in Figure 6B and Table 5.

claim: tab-1 encodes the C. elegans ortholog of the Drosophila Bsh homeobox gene and the vertebrate Bsx genes.
source: tab-1 encodes the sole C. elegans ortholog of the Drosophila Bsh homeobox gene and the vertebrate Bsx genes (Pang and Martindale, 2008).
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis cited from the literature.

claim: The GATA2/3 ortholog elt-1 affects GABA identity of D-type motor neurons.
source: The vertebrate GATA2 and GATA3 transcription factors operate as selector genes of GABAergic identity in several distinct regions of the vertebrate CNS, including the spinal cord, midbrain, forebrain and hindbrain (Achim et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2009; Kala et al., 2009; Lahti et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2010). GATA2 may act transiently after the generation of GABAergic neurons and then pass on its function to the GATA3 paralog. The sole C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate GATA2/3 is the elt-1 gene (Gillis et al., 2008), which controls early hypodermal fate patterning (Page et al., 1997). We found that an elt-1 fosmid-based reporter gene is expressed in all D-type motor neurons throughout their lifetime, but not in any other GABA-positive neuron (Figure 7A and B). Since elt-1 mutants display early embryonic lethality, we conducted a genetic mosaic analysis to examine the effect of loss of elt-1, function on D-type motor neurons, some of which generated only post-embryonically (the VD MNs). We balanced elt-1 null mutants with a fosmid that contains the elt-1 locus and an unc-47 reporter to assess the loss of the extrachromosomal array in GABAergic D-type neurons. We found that live animals that lost the rescuing array show defects in unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT and unc-46/LAMP expression in D-type neurons (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by mosaic analysis showing loss of GABA pathway gene expression in D-type neurons lacking elt-1 shown in Figure 7C.

claim: elt-1 does not affect the generation of D-type motor neurons.
source: The loss of expression of GABA markers is not a reflection of loss of the cells, since expression of unc-30, the presumptive regulatory co-factor for elt-1 is still normally expressed in the D-type neurons of elt-1 mutants (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by persistence of unc-30 expression in D-type neurons in elt-1 mutants shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The ceh-14 and ceh-17 homeobox genes control GABA identity of the ALA neuron.
source: The ceh-14 LIM homeobox gene and the ceh-17 Prd-type homeobox gene were previously shown to cooperate in the specification of several, peptidergic terminal identity features of the GABA uptake neuron ALA (Van Buskirk and Sternberg, 2010). We find that GABA staining of the ALA neurons is abrogated in ceh-14 and ceh-17 mutants (Figure 8A). Since lack of GABA staining is expected to be due to the failure to express snf-11/GAT, we crossed the snf-11/GAT fosmid reporter into ceh-14 and ceh-17 mutants and found its expression to be abrogated in the ALA neuron (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA staining and snf-11 expression in ceh-14 and ceh-17 mutants shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The Prd-type homeobox gene unc-4 controls GABA identity of the AVF neuron.
source: The AVF uptake neuron was previously shown to express the Prd-type homeobox gene unc-4 (Miller and Niemeyer, 1995). We find that unc-4 mutants do not show GABA staining in AVF and, as a likely reason for the absence of GABA staining, fail to express the snf-11/GAT transporter (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of GABA staining and snf-11 expression in unc-4 mutants shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Transcription factors that control GABAergic identity also control other identity features of the respective neurons.
source: Lastly, we set out to address the question whether factors that control GABAergic identity are committed to only control GABAergic neurotransmitter identity or whether they also control additional identity features of the respective GABAergic neurons. In other words, is the acquisition of GABAergic neurotransmitter identity coupled with the acquisition of other identity features? This appears to indeed be the case if one considers previously published results.
evidence: This is demonstrated by examining the effects of transcription factor mutations on both GABA pathway genes and other identity markers shown in Figure 9.

claim: lim-6 controls expression of nlr-1 in RIS and flp-22 in AVL.
source: We found that lim-6 also controls the expression of a more recently identified RIS marker, nlr-1, which encodes a neurexin-like gene (Haklai-Topper et al., 2011) and lim-6 affects expression of the neuropeptide-encoding flp-22 gene in the AVL neuron (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of nlr-1 and flp-22 expression in lim-6 mutants shown in Figure 9A.

claim: nhr-67 controls expression of ser-4 and nlr-1 in RIS neurons.
source: We find that in the RIS neurons, nhr-67 also controls the expression of the 5HT receptor ser-4 and of nlr-1 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of ser-4 and nlr-1 expression in nhr-67 mutants shown in Figure 9B.

claim: nhr-67 controls expression of ser-2 and avr-15 in RME neurons.
source: In the RME neurons, nhr-67 affects not only GABA identity, but also an expression of the tyramine receptor ser-2 and the Glu-gated ion channel avr-15 (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by loss of ser-2 and avr-15 expression in nhr-67 mutants shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The unc-42 homeobox gene represses GABA identity in AVK and SIB neurons.
source: In our search for additional regulators of the GABAergic phenotype, we noted that the normally peptidergic AVK neurons ectopically stain with anti-GABA antibody in animals that lack the unc-42 homeobox gene (Figure 10A). Ectopic GABA staining is accompanied by ectopic unc-25/GAD, unc-47/VGAT, unc-46/LAMP and snf-11/GAT reporter gene expression (Figure 10B). Previous work had shown that unc-42 induces the expression of multiple aspects of AVK identity (Wightman et al., 2005). It therefore appears that unc-42 promotes the peptidergic identity of AVK and suppresses an alternative GABAergic differentiation program.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ectopic GABA staining and GABA pathway gene expression in AVK and SIB in unc-42 mutants shown in Figure 10.

claim: A neurotransmitter identity has been assigned to 104 out of 118 anatomically defined neuron classes in C. elegans.
source: In total, a neurotransmitter identity has now been assigned to 104 out of the 118 anatomically defined neuron classes of the worm.
evidence: This is based on the compilation of neurotransmitter mapping data shown in Figure 11 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: 98 neuron classes employ a 'classic' fast-acting neurotransmitter (Glu, GABA, ACh).
source: 98 of these employ a 'classic' fast-acting neurotransmitter (Glu, GABA, ACh), 6 employ exclusively a monoaminergic transmitter (dopamine, serotonin, octopamine or tyramine).
evidence: This is based on the compilation of neurotransmitter mapping data.

claim: Only nine neuron classes use GABA for synaptic signaling based on anti-GABA staining and expression of the vesicular transporter.
source: Only nine neuron classes use GABA for synaptic signaling (based on anti-GABA staining and expression of the vesicular transporter) and of those, only two are pure interneurons (RIS and RIB ring interneurons; since AVB, AVA, AVJ and AVF express no known release machinery, we do not consider them as conventional GABAergic interneurons).
evidence: This is based on analysis of GABA staining and unc-47/VGAT expression patterns.

claim: Only two of the 12 ring interneuron classes utilize GABA.
source: Due to their locally restricted projections and connectivity, ring interneurons are the next closest thing to vertebrate GABAergic local inhibitory neurons. Yet only two of the 12 ring interneuron classes (collectively referred to as RI... neurons; White et al., 1986) utilize GABA.
evidence: This is based on the GABA neuron map and anatomical classification of neurons.

claim: In the male-specific tail circuitry, only one out of 20 neuron classes (the EF neuron class) constitutes a GABA neuron with conventional synthesis and release machinery.
source: In the complex male-specific tail circuitry, composed of 20 anatomically distinct neuron classes (Jarrell et al., 2012), GABA is also very sparsely used. Only one out of the 20 neuron classes, the EF neuron class, constitutes a GABA neuron with conventional synthesis and release machinery.
evidence: This is based on analysis of GABA staining and GABA pathway gene expression in male-specific neurons.

claim: The sole C. elegans GAT ortholog SNF-11 is only expressed in a small fraction of GABA-positive neurons.
source: In notable contrast, the sole C. elegans GAT ortholog SNF-11 is only expressed in a small fraction of the GABA-positive neurons and it is only expressed in two types of GABAergic targets cells (AVL as a target of DVB and body wall muscle as targets of D-type motor neurons)(this paper; (Mullen et al., 2006)).
evidence: This is based on snf-11 reporter expression patterns shown in this study.

claim: The restricted expression of SNF-11/GAT may reflect GABA spillover signaling.
source: We hypothesize that the restricted expression of SNF-11/GAT is a reflection of GABA not being immediately cleared after release, but being able to spill over to signal to non-synaptic targets.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the restricted expression pattern of snf-11 compared to vertebrate GAT expression.

claim: Some GABAergic neurons cotransmit ACh.
source: Some of the GABAergic neurons that we newly identified here cotransmit ACh (one of them, the RIB interneuron only expresses a very low level of the ACh synthesizing and transporting machinery) (Pereira et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on expression of both GABA and ACh pathway genes in these neurons.

claim: Ascaris suum displays a remarkably similar set of GABA positive neurons to C. elegans.
source: We note that Ascaris suum, a distantly related, parasitic nematode, appears to display a remarkably similar set of GABA positive neurons (Guastella et al., 1991).
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data from Ascaris suum.

claim: GABA uptake neurons exist in Ascaris suum.
source: Such GABA uptake neurons also exist in Ascaris suum (Guastella and Stretton, 1991).
evidence: This is based on published data from Ascaris suum.

claim: The genomic organization of alpha and beta subunit GABA receptor genes is conserved from nematodes to vertebrates.
source: Of particular note is the head-to-head orientation of the alpha-subunit-encoding lgc-37 gene and the beta subunit-encoding gab-1 gene (Figure 4B); strikingly, this genomic organization is conserved from nematodes to vertebrates (Darlison et al., 2005; Tsang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis and cited literature on conservation.

claim: Transcription factors that specify GABAergic phenotype act in neuron-type specific combinations.
source: Transcription factors that specify the GABAergic phenotype act in neuron-type specific combinations (Figure 9F). Each GABAergic neuron type uses its own specific combination of regulators and, hence, there is no commonly employed inducer of GABAergic identity.
evidence: This is based on the regulatory map shown in Figure 9F summarizing transcription factor requirements in different GABAergic neurons.

claim: There is reiterative use of nhr-67 and lim-6 in specifying GABA identity in different cellular contexts.
source: Nevertheless, there is a notable reiterative use of two different regulators, nhr-67 (RME, AVL, RIS) and lim-6 (AVL, RIS, DVB) in specifying GABA identity in different cellular contexts.
evidence: This is based on the expression and mutant analysis of nhr-67 and lim-6 in multiple GABAergic neuron types.

claim: The majority of regulators of neuronal identity are encoded by homeobox genes.
source: The majority of regulators of neuronal identity (of GABA, but also Glu and ACh neurons) are encoded by homeobox genes. Those that are not (nhr-67 and elt-1) cooperate with homeobox genes (Figure 9F).
evidence: This is based on the regulatory map shown in Figure 9F and Figure 12.

claim: Vertebrate GATA2/3 factors specify GABAergic identity in multiple distinct GABAergic neuron types.
source: Vertebrate GATA2/3 factors are postmitotic selectors of GABAergic identity in multiple distinct GABAergic neuron types (Achim et al., 2014; Joshi et al., 2009; Kala et al., 2009; Lahti et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate GATA factor function.

claim: A population of GABAergic neurons in the mouse CNS co-expresses the mouse orthologs of elt-1 and unc-30.
source: Remarkably, a population of GABAergic neurons in the CNS also co-expresses the mouse orthologs of elt-1 and unc-30 (Kala et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on mouse GABAergic neuron specification.

claim: In the DVB motor neuron, lim-6 controls expression of unc-25/GAD but not unc-47/VGAT or other identity features.
source: One notable exception to the coregulatory theme appears in the DVB motor neuron. GABA staining is absent in lim-6 mutants (Figure 5C) and unc-25/GAD expression is also severely affected (Figure 5C) (Hobert et al., 1999). However, neither unc-47::gfp expression (Figure 5C) nor the expression of two additional DVB markers, kal-1 and flp-10, are affected in lim-6 null mutants (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by differential effects of lim-6 mutation on different DVB markers shown in Figures 5C and 9A.

claim: lim-6 may act in a partially redundant manner with a cofactor in DVB neuron.
source: We note that in the AVL neuron, the effect of lim-6 on some markers is also very modest, but significantly enhanced if the combinatorial cofactor for lim-6 in AVL, nhr-67, is also removed (Figure 5D). We therefore suspect that lim-6 may act in a partially redundant manner with a cofactor in DVB neuron as well.
evidence: This is inferred from the synergistic effects of nhr-67 and lim-6 mutations in AVL shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The four RME neurons have very distinct lineage histories but are specified by the same terminal selector nhr-67.
source: As noted by John White more than 30 years ago, the four RME neurons are one example of a class of anatomically similar neurons whose individual class members have very distinct lineage histories (White, 1985). We have shown here that the similarity of the four RME neurons is apparently genetically programmed by a shared terminal selector, nhr-67, which appears to endow the four RME neurons its class-defining properties.
evidence: This is based on the effects of nhr-67 mutation on all four RME neurons despite their different lineages.

claim: RME subtype-specific properties are controlled by nhr-67 in collaboration with subtype-specific transcription factors.
source: RME subtype-specific properties (i.e. genes that are expressed only by a subset of the RME neurons) are also controlled by nhr-67, but the subtype-specificity is controlled by subtype-specific transcription factors that appear to collaborate with nhr-67.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of nhr-67 collaboration with ceh-10 in RMED and tab-1 in RMEL/R.

claim: Four transcription factors (unc-3, unc-42, ceh-14, unc-86) are involved in specifying the neurotransmitter identity of 46 of the 69 neuron classes for which a neurotransmitter regulatory mechanism is known.
source: This reuse is remarkable if one considers that the four most re-employed transcription factors (unc-3, unc-42, ceh-14, unc-86) are involved in specifying the neurotransmitter identity of 46 of the 69 neuron classes for which a neurotransmitter regulatory is known (Figure 12).
evidence: This is based on the system-wide regulatory map shown in Figure 12.

claim: 30-40% of all CNS synapses in vertebrates are thought to be GABAergic.
source: In vertebrates, GABA is used as a neurotransmitter by many distinct neuron types throughout the CNS (30–40% of all CNS synapses are thought to be GABAergic; [Docherty et al., 1985]) and alterations of GABAergic neurotransmission are the cause of a number of neurological diseases in humans (Webster, 2001).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate GABAergic neurotransmission.

claim: The C. elegans genome contains at least seven predicted ionotropic GABA receptors.
source: However, the C. elegans genome contains at least seven predicted ionotropic GABA receptors (Hobert, 2013) and at least some of them are expressed in cells that are not synaptically connected to the previously defined GABA neurons (Beg and Jorgensen, 2003; Jobson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on genome annotation and cited literature on GABA receptor expression.

claim: The unc-30/Pitx transcription factor selectively specifies the identity of D-type motor neurons.
source: In C. elegans, previous work has shown that the Pitx2-type transcription factor unc-30 selectively specifies the identity of D-type motor neurons along the ventral nerve cord (Cinar et al., 2005; Eastman et al., 1999; Jin et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on unc-30 function.

claim: UNC-30 protein directly controls the expression of GABA pathway genes in D-type motor neurons.
source: As a terminal selector of D-type motor neuron identity, UNC-30 protein directly controls the expression of GABA pathway genes (Eastman et al., 1999) as well as a plethora of other D-type motor neuron features (Cinar et al., 2005), including their synaptic connectivity (Howell et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on unc-30 function.

claim: unc-30 is expressed in non-GABAergic neurons.
source: Since unc-30 is expressed in non-GABAergic neurons (Jin et al., 1994), unc-30 is not sufficient to induce the GABAergic neuronal identity, possibly because unc-30 may act with as yet unknown cofactors in the D-type motor neurons.
evidence: This is based on cited literature on unc-30 expression pattern.

claim: elt-1 is a putative cofactor for unc-30 in D-type motor neurons.
source: We identify here a putative cofactor for unc-30 in the form of the elt-1 gene, the C. elegans ortholog of the vertebrate Gata2/3 transcription factors, which specify GABAergic neurons in vertebrates (Achim et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on the demonstration that elt-1 is expressed in and required for GABAergic identity of D-type motor neurons.

claim: The RIS, AVL and DVB neurons display differentiation defects in lim-6 mutant animals.
source: The acquisition of GABAergic identity of C. elegans neurons other than the D-type GABAergic motor neurons was less well understood. The RIS, AVL and DVB neurons display differentiation defects in animals lacking the lim-6 homeobox gene, the C. elegans ortholog of the vertebrate Lmx1 LIM homeobox gene (Hobert et al., 1999; Tsalik et al., 2003)
evidence: This is based on cited literature on lim-6 function.

claim: The RME neurons display differentiation defects in nhr-67 mutant animals.
source: and the RME neurons display differentiation defects in animals that either carry a mutation in the nhr-67 orphan nuclear hormone receptor, the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate Tlx/NR2E1 gene and the fly gene Tailless (Sarin et al., 2009)
evidence: This is based on cited literature on nhr-67 function.

claim: The RME neurons display differentiation defects in ceh-10 mutant animals.
source: or in animals lacking ceh-10, the C. elegans ortholog of the vertebrate Vsx/Chx10 Prd-type homeobox gene (Forrester et al., 1998; Huang et al., 2004).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on ceh-10 function.

claim: nhr-67 controls all GABAergic identity features in AVL, RIS, RMEL/R, and RMED/V motor neurons.
source: We show here that nhr-67 controls all GABAergic identity features in the AVL, RIS and RMEL/R and RMED/V motor neurons, where it collaborates with distinct homeobox genes, lim-6 in AVL and RIS, ceh-10 in RMED and a novel transcription factor, tab-1, the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate Bsx, in RMEL/R.
evidence: This is based on the mutant analysis of nhr-67 and its collaborating factors shown in the manuscript.

claim: tab-1 is the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate Bsx.
source: We show here that nhr-67 controls all GABAergic identity features in the AVL, RIS and RMEL/R and RMED/V motor neurons, where it collaborates with distinct homeobox genes, lim-6 in AVL and RIS, ceh-10 in RMED and a novel transcription factor, tab-1, the C. elegans ortholog of vertebrate Bsx, in RMEL/R.
evidence: This is based on sequence homology analysis.

claim: Drosophila Bsh has been implicated in the specification of several neuron types in the Drosophila optic lobe.
source: Drosophila Bsh has been implicated in the specification of several neuron types in the Drosophila optic lobe (Hasegawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on Drosophila Bsh function.

claim: A subset of Drosophila optic lobe neurons specified by Bsh are GABAergic.
source: A subset of these neurons are GABAergic (Raghu et al., 2013), indicating that a function of Bsh-type homeobox genes in the specification of the GABAergic phenotype may be phylogenetically conserved.
evidence: This is based on cited literature on Drosophila neuron types.

claim: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons in vertebrates take up GABA via GAT1 and GAT4 and then release GABA.
source: While further studies are required to test the concept of 'GABA recycling neurons' in C. elegans, we note an interesting precedent of GABA recycling in the vertebrate CNS. Midbrain dopaminergic neurons do not synthesize GABA, but take it up via the GABA transporters GAT1 and GAT4 and then release GABA to inhibit postsynaptic neurons (Tritsch et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate dopaminergic neurons.

claim: Some vertebrate glial cell types employ GABA as a 'gliotransmitter'.
source: In vertebrates, some glial cell types are thought to employ GABA as a 'gliotransmitter', releasing GABA via a reversal of the plasma membrane GABA transporter GAT-1 to signal to neurons (Barakat and Bordey, 2002; Koch and Magnusson, 2009; Yoon and Lee, 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate glial GABA signaling.

claim: The bestrophin ion channel mediates GABA release from glia in vertebrates.
source: For example, the bestrophin ion channel has been shown to mediate GABA release from glia (Lee et al., 2010) and there are multiple, uncharacterized bestrophin genes in the C. elegans genome (Hobert, 2013).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate glial GABA release mechanisms.

claim: Passive transfer of neurotransmitters through gap junctions occurs in amacrine and bipolar cells of the vertebrate retina.
source: The passive transfer of neurotransmitters through gap junctions has been termed 'neurotransmitter coupling' and occurs, for example, in the amacrine and bipolar cells of the vertebrate retina (Vaney et al., 1998).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate retinal neurotransmission.

claim: Spinal cord motor neurons in the rat take up GABA but do not synthesize it.
source: For example, spinal cord motor neurons in the rat do not synthesize GABA but take up GABA after its release from presynaptic neurons (Snow et al., 1992).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on rat spinal cord motor neurons.

claim: The vertebrate CNS contains neurons that do not synthesize GABA but take it up via GAT.
source: Whether analogous GABA clearance neurons exist in the vertebrate CNS is as yet unclear, but it is notable that the vertebrate CNS does contain neurons that do not synthesize GABA but take it up via GAT (Conti et al., 2004; Swan et al., 1994).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate GABA uptake.

claim: In vertebrates, most GABA-positive neurons express GAT (GAT1 or GAT3).
source: In vertebrates, these transporters are expressed widely throughout the CNS, with most GABA-positive neurons also expressing GAT (GAT1 or GAT3); many postsynaptic targets of vertebrate GABAergic neurons also express GAT (Conti et al., 2004; Swan et al., 1994; Zhou and Danbolt, 2013).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate GAT expression.

claim: ACh/GABA-cotransmitting neurons have been observed in multiple neuron types of the vertebrate CNS.
source: ACh/GABA-cotransmitting neurons have been observed in multiple neuron types of the vertebrate CNS as well (Granger et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate cotransmission.

claim: Neurons that use two neurotransmitters can package both into the same vesicles or package them separately into spatially segregated presynaptic zones.
source: Neurons that use two neurotransmitters can, in principle, package both neurotransmitters into the same vesicles or package them separately into spatially segregated presynaptic zones (Vaaga et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on cotransmission mechanisms.

claim: GABAergic disinhibition is a common organizational principle of inhibitory circuits in the vertebrate CNS.
source: This observation suggests that so-called 'GABAergic disinhibition' (=GABA-mediated inhibition of an inhibitory GABA neuron), a common organizational principle of inhibitory circuits in the vertebrate CNS (Roberts, 1974), may also be broadly occurring in the C. elegans nervous system.
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate GABAergic circuits and inference from C. elegans connectivity data.

claim: GABA spillover transmission occurs in the vertebrate CNS and in C. elegans.
source: These receptors may simply not function as GABA receptors or, more interestingly, these receptors may mediate GABA spillover transmission, a phenomenon observed in the vertebrate CNS as well as in C. elegans (Jobson et al., 2015; Rossi and Hamann, 1998).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on GABA spillover transmission.

claim: Vertebrate GABAT has a very broad tissue distribution.
source: We find a fosmid-based reporter of gta-1 to be ubiquitously expressed (Figure 2D), which mirrors the very broad tissue distribution of vertebrate GABAT and is consistent with GABAT using substrates other than GABA (Jeremiah and Povey, 1981).
evidence: This is based on cited literature on vertebrate GABAT and comparison with C. elegans gta-1 expression.
